title: Everything about boycotting Danone: from supporting Israel to its official presence in Iran
summary: An introduction to Danone, documentation of its support for Israel and its presence in the Iranian market, citing official sources.

data.text: "Danone": a French dessert with Hebrew garnish

You've certainly heard the name "Danette" before. Milk-based desserts that have for years been carving a place in Iranian families' shopping baskets as a healthy, tasty snack for children. And if you've had to deal with a newborn you definitely recognise names like "Aptamil" and "Bebelac" in the infant-formula market — formulas that, alongside Nestlé products, are the best-sellers of the Iranian formula market. These are a portion of the products of the multinational mega-corporation "Danone" that have an official presence in our country's market. A mega-corporation that has always been one of the supporters of Israel, a fixture on every boycott list of pro-Palestinian movements. But is Danone really, as they say, a supporter of and connected to the Israelis? When we put a spoonful of cold, fresh French dessert in our mouths and enjoy its delicious taste, do we really need to worry about helping Israel's economy? Stay with us as we examine this strange claim.
Part one: I invest, therefore I am!

Danone is one of the largest food companies in the world. According to the company's financial documents, in 2023 — with €27.6 billion in worldwide sales — it ranked first among companies in dairy, plant-based and beverages; second in bottled waters and infant nutrition; and fourth in adult food. (Danone website). But how has this food giant ended up on the Zionist-goods boycott list?

The story begins with Danone's interest in investing in Israeli companies. For example, in a single round in 2023 Danone invested $4 million in a newly founded Israeli technology company called "Wilk". (The Jerusalem Post). This start-up's field is producing dairy products via the cells that produce them. You might say $4 million is not a big number for a multi-billion-dollar company. You'd be right! Although for a new start-up it's a notable sum, in fact what matters more about this investment than the amount is something else:

"An investment of about $4 million in an Israeli tech company — even when investment in the local tech sector has dropped sharply — is not [much of a] big deal. But this time, instead of the amount, it is the identity of the investors that is notable. So this funding round for the tech firm Wilk can be called a commercial breakthrough."
data.caption: Source: The Jerusalem Post

data.text: The Jerusalem Post columnist explains the importance of this investment well. The data shows that the rate of foreign investment in Israel, despite many incentives in recent years, has been wave-like. The figure in Q1 2023 was around $1.7 billion — the lowest level since 2019. (Science Business). Internal disagreements over judicial reforms appear to have been the main reason for this drop:

"We are in the middle of a global crisis today and it's still too early to know when and how [this crisis] will end. A local crisis has been added on top of this, creating even more uncertainty [for investors]. [Even] if the judicial crisis is resolved, [it will still] take time to get out of it — and even then, rebuilding investor trust takes time."
data.caption: Dror Bin / CEO, Israel Innovation Authority — Source: Science Business

data.text: Now imagine that in the middle of this crisis and the hesitation of foreign investors, a reputable name like Danone steps in with a few million dollars to turn the page and reassure hesitant investors (just like celebrities do for you in TV commercials for famous brands). The widespread coverage of this investment in Israeli media is due to precisely this advertising value.

data.caption: Using familiar faces in commercial ads [top] / Wide coverage of Danone's investment in Israeli media, emphasising the credibility of the investor [bottom]

data.text: Less than a month later Danone made a similar investment in another Israeli start-up, "ImaginDairy" (The Times of Israel), showing that its investment in Israel was not an exception but a rule. But does the story of Danone and Israel begin in 2023 and is it limited to investing in Israeli start-ups?

data.caption: "Wilk" and "ImaginDairy": Danone's most recent investments on the Danone Ventures website

data.text: Part two: "Strauss": Danone in Hebrew!

Danone's interest in investing in Israel goes back 55 years. In 1969 Danone signed a cooperation agreement with an Israeli food company called "Strauss". That year Strauss got access to Danone's production knowledge and also took over distribution of various Danone products in Israel. In 1972 Danone and Strauss opened a new factory in Israel and began producing the "Dani" brand (which is our "Danette"), which brought significant success for both companies. (Strauss website).

data.caption: The start of Strauss and Danone's cooperation in the company's timeline on the Strauss website

data.text: An unbreakable bond

After a decade of successful cooperation, in 1982 — to stay safe from the "Arab boycott of Israeli goods" — Danone decided to end the partnership. That separation lasted 14 years, until in 1996, after the Arab-boycott danger had passed, Danone returned with a big investment, this time acquiring 20% of Strauss Dairy. Strauss refers to this as "the great return".

data.caption: The story of Danone's "great return" to cooperation with Strauss

data.text: The Strauss website considers this move an effective factor in facilitating innovation and growth at Strauss, as well as in producing and selling Danone products via this Israeli company:

"Our activity in Israel is accompanied by a set of strategic partnerships with global food manufacturers; the Danone Group owns 20% of Strauss Dairy, and PepsiCo is a 50% partner in our salty snacks. These constructive long-term partnerships have enabled us to build extensive and stable professional and commercial infrastructure."
data.caption: Source: Strauss website

data.text: But what had Strauss done that Danone, fearing the Arab boycott, gave up the partnership for 14 years?
Israel is my home!

"Israel is our true home, a wellspring of culture that became the foundation of our value-driven work and professional knowledge. Israel's largest food company was born with a Zionist ideology, love of homeland(!) and generosity."
data.caption: Source: Strauss website

data.text: This is part of Strauss's self-introduction on its own official website. Strauss, which by its own description is Israel's largest food company and the leader of the Israeli food market, has been active in the occupied territories for over 80 years; some 6,500 people work at its more than 20 production sites across occupied Palestine. According to its own website, Strauss has always kept over 50% of its turnover inside Israel. (Strauss website)
What's interesting about Strauss is precisely these sharp political and ideological attitudes. Strauss truly considers itself a Zionist brand committed to Israel's ideals.

data.caption: Strauss products in the hands of Zionist soldiers in the company's promotional video

data.text: Despite Strauss's international operations, the Israeli flag and images of Zionist soldiers appear all over the company's website. After the clashes following 7 October 2023 [Operation Al-Aqsa Storm], Strauss launched a campaign called "Always Together". On the website's front page, under this very campaign, promotional images of Zionist soldiers celebrating with the company's products are displayed.
The company's promotional video introducing the "Always Together" campaign

Across various pages about this campaign, the company's commitment to supporting settlers within range of Hamas rockets — and to not shutting down operations in areas near Gaza — is emphasised. Strauss has also supported residents displaced from war zones. (Strauss website). These pages also extensively mention occupied settlements where Strauss has some kind of presence and operations, including a chip-production factory in Sderot (Strauss website). More strikingly, at the bottom of every page of the company's website there's a countdown for the release of Israeli hostages in Gaza.

"As a company whose roots have grown from the very history of the country(!) of Israel, our products and brands have a strong connection with [Israeli] consumers, accompany them in their daily lives, and are a central part of recognition in every [Israeli] home."
data.caption: Source: Strauss website

data.text: According to its own account, Strauss helped the Israeli army during the fourth Arab-Israeli war (the Yom Kippur war) in 1973 as well. In a section of the company's history titled "At the war front, at the front lines of the economy", Strauss mentions running its production lines 24 hours a day during the war to meet the military's needs. The reason Strauss was placed on the Arab boycott list was precisely this active participation in wars.
OK, so what does Danone's partnership with Strauss and its investment in Israeli start-ups have to do with us, Iranian consumers? Are we Iranians also Danone customers?
Part three: Just find its smile!

data.caption: Danone's advertising campaign to differentiate its products from competitors

data.text: Danone France began its activities in Iran in 2007 (1386) through the establishment of Danone Sahar in cooperation with Sahar Dairy. This presence initially started with importing products. From 2009 (1388) Danone Sahar also began producing Danone products in Iran. You can see the full history of Danone's presence in Iran here on the company's own website. In 2015 (1394) Danone continued its presence in Iran under the name Danone Lebani Pars.

data.caption: According to Danone's official documents, 100% of the ownership of "Danone Lebani Pars" belongs to Danone.
The Danette family is Danone's best-known product in the Iranian market.

data.text: In addition to dairy products, Danone has a strong presence in Iran in two other areas: bottled water and infant formula and baby food. From 2009 (1388) to 2021 (1400) Danone owned Damavand mineral water, but with the 2021 investment by the French company Fromineust, and given the company's recent announcements, Danone no longer appears to hold a significant share in that company.

However, in the infant-formula industry, 60% of the shares of Mashhad Milk Powder Industries (Nutricia MMP) belong to Danone. (Danone's official 2023 report). Danone's activity in child-nutrition runs through its subsidiaries — that is, Nutricia and Milupa. In fact, Nutricia MMP is Danone Nutricia's representative in Iran.

data.caption: The "About Us" section on the Mashhad Milk Powder Industries website

data.text: Danone is present in Iran's infant-formula market with two brands: Aptamil and Bebelac Milupa. The products mentioned are produced at the Mashhad Milk Powder Industries factory.

data.caption: Aptamil, a Milupa product, and Bebelac, a Nutricia product — both subsidiaries of Danone.

data.text: An economic Iron Dome

You may have heard of Israel's air-defence system — the system designed to neutralise the impact of rockets, drones and missiles launched towards Israel. This is exactly what the likes of Danone do for Israel's economy. Every time internal problems or war strike a blow to Israel's economy, Danone — with its backing and investment — neutralises that blow. Danone has previously, once, been forced to retreat from its ties to the Zionists for 14 years. Is it possible this happens again?

Now, when you're enjoying the taste of French dessert or preparing Aptamil or Bebelac infant formula for your baby, you'll better understand its connection to Israel's economy — a connection that every Iranian consumer has the right to know.
